title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
In this post, I explore the Palmer Penguins dataset using R. I will compare body mass across penguin species and investigate how bill measurements differ between species.
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
The Palmer Penguins dataset was collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program. The dataset is available under the CC0 licence.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Understanding the dataset
I first check the size of the dataset and count the missing values in each variable.

cat("Number of observations:", nrow(penguins), "\n")

Number of observations: 344 

cat("Number of variables:", ncol(penguins), "\n")

Number of variables: 8 

colSums(is.na(penguins))

          species            island    bill_length_mm     bill_depth_mm 
                0                 0                 2                 2 
flipper_length_mm       body_mass_g               sex              year 
                2                 2                11                 0 


The dataset contains measurements for individual penguins from three species. Some variables contain missing observations, so these need to be considered before calculating summaries.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Preparing the data
For this analysis, I focus on species, body mass, bill length, and bill depth. I remove rows that have missing values in any of these variables.

analysis_penguins <- penguins[
  complete.cases(
    penguins[, c("species", "body_mass_g", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")]
  ),
  c("species", "body_mass_g", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")
]

cat("Rows before removing missing values:", nrow(penguins), "\n")

Rows before removing missing values: 344 

cat("Rows after removing missing values:", nrow(analysis_penguins), "\n")

Rows after removing missing values: 342 

head(analysis_penguins)

  species body_mass_g bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm
1  Adelie        3750           39.1          18.7
2  Adelie        3800           39.5          17.4
3  Adelie        3250           40.3          18.0
5  Adelie        3450           36.7          19.3
6  Adelie        3650           39.3          20.6
7  Adelie        3625           38.9          17.8


Removing incomplete observations ensures that the summaries and plots below are based on penguins with all of the measurements required for this analysis.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Comparing species
Next, I calculate the average body mass, bill length, and bill depth for each penguin species.

species_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(body_mass_g, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) ~ species,
  data = analysis_penguins,
  FUN = mean
)

species_summary[, -1] <- round(species_summary[, -1], 1)

species_summary

    species body_mass_g bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm
1    Adelie      3700.7           38.8          18.3
2 Chinstrap      3733.1           48.8          18.4
3    Gentoo      5076.0           47.5          15.0


The summary shows that the three species differ in their typical body measurements. Gentoo penguins have the greatest average body mass, while the species also show noticeable differences in average bill length and bill depth.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Body mass by species
To see the differences in body mass more clearly, I create a boxplot for the three penguin species.

boxplot(
  body_mass_g ~ species,
  data = analysis_penguins,
  xlab = "Species",
  ylab = "Body mass (g)",
  main = "Body mass by penguin species"
)







Figure 1: Distribution of body mass across the three Palmer penguin species.





The figure shows clear differences in body mass among the species. Gentoo penguins tend to have higher body mass values than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Relationship between bill measurements
Finally, I calculate the correlation between bill length and bill depth separately for each species.

bill_correlations <- sapply(
  split(analysis_penguins, analysis_penguins$species),
  function(group) {
    cor(group$bill_length_mm, group$bill_depth_mm)
  }
)

round(bill_correlations, 3)

   Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
    0.391     0.654     0.643 


These values show how bill length and bill depth are related within each species. Calculating the correlations separately avoids mixing the three species together when examining this relationship.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins with R
text:
Conclusion
This analysis used R to explore differences in body and bill measurements among Palmer penguin species. After checking for missing data and preparing a complete dataset, I compared average measurements across species and visualized the distribution of body mass.
The results show clear differences among Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. Gentoo penguins are heavier on average, and the species also differ in their bill measurements. The analysis demonstrates how data cleaning, summary statistics, visualization, and correlation can be used to explore a biological dataset in R.

Understanding the dataset
Before comparing the penguin species, I first examine the size of the dataset, the available variables, and the amount of missing data.

The dataset contains measurements and identifying information for individual penguins. Checking the missing values is important because incomplete observations could affect calculations involving body measurements.
I will focus on species, flipper length, and body mass. I remove observations that are missing either of the two numerical measurements needed for the analysis.

analysis_penguins = (
    penguins[
        ["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]

)

Comparing the penguin species
Next, I calculate the number of penguins and the average flipper length and body mass for each species.

species_summary = (

    .groupby("species")
    .agg(
        number_of_penguins=("species", "size"),
        mean_flipper_length_mm=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"),
        mean_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean")
    )
    .round(1)
)

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins with Python
section: Relationship between flipper length and body mass
text:
Relationship between flipper length and body mass
To investigate whether larger penguins tend to have longer flippers, I plot flipper length against body mass and distinguish the points by species.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

for species, group in analysis_penguins.groupby("species", observed=True):
    ax.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Body mass and flipper length by species")
ax.legend(title="Species")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Relationship between flipper length and body mass for Palmer penguins.





The plot shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass. Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass. The species also form distinct groups, with Gentoo penguins tending to be both heavier and longer-flippered than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins with Python
text:
Measuring the relationship
The scatter plot suggests that flipper length and body mass are positively related. I calculate the correlation between these two measurements for each species to quantify that relationship.

correlations = (
    analysis_penguins
    .groupby("species")
    .apply(
        lambda group: group["flipper_length_mm"].corr(group["body_mass_g"]),
        include_groups=False
    )
    .rename("correlation")
    .round(3)
)

correlations

species
Adelie       0.468
Chinstrap    0.642
Gentoo       0.703
Name: correlation, dtype: float64


A positive correlation means that penguins with longer flippers also tend to have greater body mass within that species. Comparing the values across the three species shows whether this relationship is similar or different among Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins with Python
text:
Conclusion
This analysis explored body measurements in the Palmer Penguins dataset using Python. After checking and cleaning the data, I compared average flipper length and body mass across species and visualized the relationship between these two measurements.
The results show clear differences in body size among the penguin species. The scatter plot and correlation calculations also show that flipper length and body mass are positively associated within the data. Overall, the analysis demonstrates how data cleaning, grouping, summary statistics, and visualization can be used together to investigate patterns in a biological dataset.
